what_its_for: Avatrombopag is used to treat low platelet counts (called thrombocytopenia) in adults. Platelets are tiny blood cells that help your blood clot. This medicine is used in two situations: (1) before a medical procedure in adults with chronic liver disease who have low platelets, and (2) for adults with a condition called chronic immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) when other treatments have not worked well enough.
how_to_take: Take avatrombopag by mouth with food. Swallow the tablets whole — do not crush, split, or chew them. Always take this medicine with a meal to help it work properly. Try to take it at the same time each day.
dosing: Your dose depends on why you are taking this medicine and your platelet count. For chronic liver disease before a procedure, the usual dose is 40 mg or 60 mg once daily for 5 days, based on your platelet count — your doctor will decide which dose is right for you. For chronic ITP, the usual starting dose is 20 mg once daily. Your doctor may adjust your dose over time based on how your platelet counts respond. Never change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if you still have time to take it with food that same day. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose as scheduled. Do not take two doses on the same day to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store avatrombopag tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the tablets in their original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep this medicine away from moisture, heat, and direct light. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking avatrombopag with certain antifungal medicines (like fluconazole or itraconazole) or rifampin unless your doctor knows about it, as these can change how much medicine gets into your body. Tell your doctor and pharmacist about ALL medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements you take. Avoid activities that could cause bleeding or bruising while your platelet count is very low. Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you notice: unusual or excessive bleeding (such as bleeding gums, nosebleeds, blood in your urine or stool, or heavier than normal menstrual bleeding); signs of a blood clot, such as pain, swelling, or redness in your leg, sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, or sudden numbness or weakness on one side of your body; signs of a serious liver problem, such as yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain; or if your platelet count drops very low again after stopping treatment. Also let your doctor know if you become pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
when_it_works: For chronic liver disease patients preparing for a procedure, your platelet count should start to increase within a few days, usually reaching its highest level about 10 to 13 days after starting treatment. For chronic ITP, it may take a few weeks to see the full benefit as your doctor adjusts your dose to find the right level for you. Your doctor will check your blood regularly to monitor your platelet count.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: It is not known if this medicine is safe during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Talk to your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Older adults (65 and over): No special dose adjustment is needed, but your doctor will monitor you closely. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor will decide if any dose adjustments are needed based on your specific condition. This medicine is not approved for use in children.
